questions.q: List the five psychosexual stages in correct developmental order and give the approximate age range for each.
questions.a: Oral (0‑18 months), Anal (18‑36 months), Phallic (3‑6 years), Latency (6‑12 years), Genital (puberty onward). A wrong order or missing stage indicates the student has not memorised the basic sequence; missing age ranges suggests they cannot anchor stages to developmental milestones, which is essential for case‑based questions.

questions.q: A 30‑year‑old chain‑smoker who constantly chews pens and makes sarcastic remarks when stressed is described by a friend as “orally fixated.” Explain in your own words what “oral fixation” means and why these specific behaviours fit that label.
questions.a: Oral fixation occurs when an infant’s needs for sucking/feeding are either over‑gratified or frustrated, causing libido to remain anchored to the mouth. The adult then seeks oral stimulation (smoking, chewing) and uses sarcasm (verbal aggression) as a symbolic re‑enactment of early biting. If the student merely says “they like oral things” without linking to early weaning conflict or the pleasure principle, they confuse fixation with simple habit.

questions.q: A preschooler refuses to let anyone else flush the toilet after a bowel movement, insisting on doing it themselves, and throws tantrums if interrupted. Using Freud’s theory, identify the stage, the erogenous zone, the core conflict, and the two possible adult personality outcomes if fixation occurs.
questions.a: Stage: Anal (18‑36 months). Erogenous zone: anus/bowel. Core conflict: toilet training — balancing id’s pleasure in expulsion/retention with ego/superego demands for control. Fixation outcomes: anal‑retentive (excessive orderliness, stinginess, stubbornness) or anal‑expulsive (messiness, destructiveness, cruelty). A student who only names “anal stage” without describing the dual fixation outcomes or the role of parental training style has not applied the concept fully.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the Oedipus complex in boys and the Electra complex in girls. Include the role of castration anxiety and penis envy, and explain how each is resolved through identification with the same‑sex parent.
questions.a: Both complexes occur in the phallic stage (3‑6 years) when children discover genital differences. Boy: desires mother, sees father as rival, fears castration → resolves by identifying with father, internalising his authority (superego formation). Girl: desires father, blames mother for “castration” (penis envy), shifts love to father → resolves by identifying with mother, hoping to share father’s affection later. A student who treats them as identical or omits the asymmetric anxiety (castration vs. penis envy) misses Freud’s controversial but exam‑critical gender distinction.

questions.q: Critically evaluate the claim: “Freud’s psychosexual stages are universally valid because they are based on biological maturation.” Use at least two arguments from the textbook’s criticisms of psychodynamic theories.
questions.a: The claim is weak. (1) Freud’s theory relies on case studies of a narrow, upper‑class Viennese sample, not cross‑cultural data. (2) Concepts like “penis envy” reflect Victorian gender bias, not universal biology. (3) The stages are not empirically testable — fixation cannot be directly observed. A student who simply agrees because “biology drives development” ignores the textbook’s explicit criticisms about lack of scientific rigour and male‑centred prototype.

questions.q: Create a short original case vignette (3‑4 sentences) of an adult showing clear latency‑stage fixation. Describe the behaviours and explain why they indicate unresolved latency conflicts rather than phallic or genital issues.
questions.a: Example: “Ravi, 28, avoids all romantic relationships. He spends evenings alone mastering chess strategies and collecting stamps, feeling intense anxiety when peers discuss dating. He has no sexual interest but also no Oedipal jealousy toward his father.” This shows latency fixation because energy remains channelled into asexual, skill‑based activities (substituted for dormant sexuality) without the phallic stage’s parental rivalry or genital stage’s mature heterosexual interest. A poor answer would describe mere shyness or asexuality without linking to the stage’s hallmark: sublimation of sexual urges into intellectual/social pursuits.
